To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the incorporation of information on time of HIV diagnosis in backcalculation models of the AIDS epidemic in England and Wales does not change the estimates of the number of HIV infections in the population and that the estimates of the rate of diagnosis of HIV infection among infected individuals in the different exposure groups are similar to the estimates obtained by using the AIDS data only, with the exception of the estimates for the heterosexual group, which are lower when HIV diagnosis information is incorporated.

(1) the use of information on the date of HIV diagnosis in AIDS surveillance data allows the estimation of HIV diagnosis rates among HIV-infected persons and (2) these diagnosis rates are lower than the rates estimated by using the number of AIDS cases in a group and assuming all HIV-infected persons in that group develop AIDS.
the incorporation of HIV diagnosis information into backcalculations is feasible, and that it is possible to estimate the rate at which HIV infection is diagnosed among HIV-infected persons.

the use of information on the time of HIV diagnosis in monitoring AIDS incidence is feasible and can be used to improve estimates of the number of undiagnosed HIV infections.
